plans.label: Steady
plans.headline: Invest 35,000 a month, weighted towards debt
plans.body: This plan puts 40% of your monthly investment into equity and 60% into debt, and reaches a projected 2,660,000 against your 2,500,000 target in five years. It asks for 35,000 of your 45,000 monthly surplus, which leaves you 10,000 of breathing room each month. Out of 10,000 simulations run on real historical market returns, 7,376 reached your goal. It does not survive our stress test: "Unexpected major vehicle repair", "Refrigerator or AC replacement" and "Urgent plumbing or roof repair" landing together would leave you 5,000 short of the goal.

plans.label: Growth
plans.headline: Invest 52,000 a month, mostly in equity
plans.body: This plan puts 85% of your monthly investment into equity and 15% into debt, and reaches a projected 4,410,000 against your 2,500,000 target in five years. It is not affordable on your current finances: it needs 52,000 a month against a surplus of 45,000, leaving you 7,000 short every month. Out of 10,000 simulations run on real historical market returns, 9,240 reached your goal. It also held up against every combination of shock events we tested.

goal_priority_note: Your house downpayment is funded first because it is five years away, while the child education goal is twelve years out and can absorb a slower start. The nearer deadline is the binding one, so it sets the monthly figure.
mismatch_note: You described your approach as aggressive, but your transaction history looks moderate. On two occasions you sold equity within days of a market fall. That matters here because the plans with the highest projected returns are exactly the ones that fall furthest during a bad year, and a plan left early performs worse than a slower plan held to the end.
